steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our HCI paper proposing a spatial constraint model that lets people interactively manipulate static visualizations. Cover why static visualizations are a problem, the idea of the model, the prototype system and user study, and end with the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Interaction matters, but many visualizations are static
- Spatial change as the core of many interactions; proposal of a spatial constraint model
- How the model works: visual objects under physical constraints
- Prototype system, supported tasks, evaluation
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Interaction matters, but many visualizations are static
  - interaction = dialogue between users and visualizations; alternative representations, perspectives in data exploration
  - many real-world visualizations static or limited interaction
  - creators: paper-based practices; specialized programming knowledge (D^{3}, Vega, ECharts)
  - users: complex interaction needs beyond predefined options
- Spatial change
  - interaction process = user actions + visualization changes
  - spatial channel among most perceptually effective visual channels -> spatial change most prevalent
  - examples: grouped -> stacked bar chart re-encoding; stacking order of a ThemeRiver; change position, shape, size
  - propose spatial constraint model: constraints on visual objects, enables interaction with original static visualizations
- How the model works
  - visual objects (points, bars, areas) as entities governed by physical principles
  - constraints: gravity, support, collision, fixation; integrated to build intricate interactions
  - vs. conventional tool kits (e.g., D3): position/shape = outcome of pre-programmed functions; ours = physical perspective
  - spatial updates activated by interactions; stable positions = equilibrium of constraints (object equilibrium)
- Prototype system
  - interactive manipulation of existing visualizations; converge to new layouts
  - tasks: drag to reorder (stacking order, orientation), zoom/drag scales, add or modify constraints
  - analysis tasks: navigation, filtering, reordering, re-encoding, aggregation
  - constraints -> forces; force-directed optimization -> new layout
  - bar, area, bubble, line charts
  - real-world examples + user studies; participants with varying expertise; intuitive, easy to understand; novices and experts
- Contributions
  - spatial constraint model (positions + positional changes, intuitive transitions)
  - prototype system for activating and manipulating static visualizations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Interaction is very important for the dialogue between users and visualizations, since it gives alternative representations and different perspectives while exploring data. But even though it is important, many visualizations in the real world are static or only have limited interaction. This comes from both the creators and the users. For creators, traditional paper-based practices and the specialized knowledge you need for visualization programming (with tools like D^{3}, Vega, or ECharts) lead to visualizations without interactivity. For users, complex interaction needs that go beyond the predefined options can also make interactive visualizations hard to realize.

A full interaction process includes both the user actions and the changes in the visualization. One of the most common types of change is spatial change, because the spatial channel is one of the most perceptually effective visual channels. So many interactions can be seen as spatial changes to elements in the visualization. For example, re-encoding a grouped bar chart into a stacked bar chart, or changing the stacking order of a ThemeRiver, are both spatial transformations in the visualization that change the position, shape or size of visual elements. Since static visualizations are so common and could benefit from interaction, we propose a spatial constraint model to make spatial interactions in visualizations possible. The model defines spatial constraints on the visual objects in the visualization, which lets users interact with the original static visualizations and supports a wide range of interactions with them.

- How the model works
  - visual objects (points, bars, areas) governed by physical principles
  - gravity, support, collision, fixation constraints, combined for intricate interactions
  - vs. tool kits like D3 (pre-programmed functions) -> physical perspective; updates triggered by interactions
  - stable position = equilibrium of constraints
- Prototype system
  - manipulate existing visualizations, converge to new layouts
  - dragging to reorder, zoom/drag scales, add/modify constraints -> navigation, filtering, reordering, re-encoding, aggregation
  - constraints -> forces, force-directed optimization
  - bar, area, bubble, line charts; examples + user studies; novices and experts
- Contributions
  - spatial constraint model
  - prototype system

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Interaction is very important for the dialogue between users and visualizations, since it gives alternative representations and different perspectives while exploring data. But even though it is important, many visualizations in the real world are static or only have limited interaction. This comes from both the creators and the users. For creators, traditional paper-based practices and the specialized knowledge you need for visualization programming (with tools like D^{3}, Vega, or ECharts) lead to visualizations without interactivity. For users, complex interaction needs that go beyond the predefined options can also make interactive visualizations hard to realize.

A full interaction process includes both the user actions and the changes in the visualization. One of the most common types of change is spatial change, because the spatial channel is one of the most perceptually effective visual channels. So many interactions can be seen as spatial changes to elements in the visualization. For example, re-encoding a grouped bar chart into a stacked bar chart, or changing the stacking order of a ThemeRiver, are both spatial transformations in the visualization that change the position, shape or size of visual elements. Since static visualizations are so common and could benefit from interaction, we propose a spatial constraint model to make spatial interactions in visualizations possible. The model defines spatial constraints on the visual objects in the visualization, which lets users interact with the original static visualizations and supports a wide range of interactions with them.

In the spatial constraint model we think of visual objects (points, bars, areas, etc.) as entities that follow physical principles. A set of spatial constraints applies to these visual objects, including gravity, support, collision and fixation constraints. The constraints are combined to build intricate interactions, and they are the basis for the sequence of visual object updates that interactions trigger. Conventional tool kits (e.g., D3) treat the position and shape of visual objects as the outcome of pre-programmed functions, but we take a physical perspective to model the spatial channels of visual objects. The key point is that our approach introduces spatial updates that are triggered by interactions. From this point of view, the stable position of the visual objects comes from the equilibrium reached by the interplay of the spatial constraints, which is inspired by the idea of object equilibrium.

To validate the model, we developed a prototype system for interactively manipulating existing visualizations. After manipulation, the visualizations are transformed and converge to new layouts, which helps users explore the visualization and the underlying data. The interactions support a range of user tasks, for example reordering visual objects by dragging to change stacking orders or orientations, zooming or dragging scales to reorganize or rescale axes, and adding new constraints or modifying the existing ones. These operations make intelligent interactions possible for user analysis tasks like navigation, filtering, reordering, re-encoding and aggregation. After the user interacts with the visualization, our system maps the spatial constraints to forces and pushes the visual objects toward convergent positions with force-directed optimization. When they converge, a new visualization layout comes out. The model can be applied to various common visualization types, such as bar charts, area charts, bubble charts and line charts. We show that our approach works for supporting diverse interactive tasks for common visualizations through real-world examples and user studies. We ran user experiments with participants with different levels of expertise in visualization. The experiments showed that the interactions supported by the spatial constraint model are intuitive and easy to understand and can support diverse forms of interaction. So our approach is useful for both novice and expert users. The contributions of this work are:

- A spatial constraint model that represents both the positions and the position changes of visual objects, and also allows intuitive transitions after users manipulate visualizations.

- A prototype system based on the constraint model, which lets users activate and manipulate static visualizations.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Interaction plays a crucial role in facilitating a dialogue between users and visualizations, providing alternative representations and different perspectives during data exploration. Despite its importance, many real-world visualizations are static or have limited interactive capabilities. This issue arises from both the creators' and the users' perspectives. On the creators' side, traditional paper-based practices and the specialized knowledge required for visualization programming (using tools like D^{3} [1], Vega [2], or ECharts [3]) contribute to the lack of interactivity. On the users' side, complex interaction requirements beyond the predefined options can also hinder the realization of interactive visualizations.

A comprehensive interaction process encompasses both user actions and visualization changes. Spatial change is one of the most prevalent types of change, given that the spatial channel is one of the most perceptually effective visual channels [4]. Therefore, many interactions can be categorized as spatial changes affecting elements within the visualization. For example, re-encoding a grouped bar chart as a stacked bar chart and changing the stacking order of a ThemeRiver [5] are both spatial transformations within the visualization, altering the position, shape, or size of visual elements. Considering the prevalence of static visualizations and their potential benefits from interaction, we propose a spatial constraint model that facilitates spatial interactions within visualizations. The model defines spatial constraints on visual objects within the visualization, enabling user interactions with the original static visualizations and supporting a wide range of interactions with them.

In the spatial constraint model, we conceptualize visual objects (such as points, bars, areas, etc.) as entities governed by physical principles. These visual objects are subject to a set of spatial constraints, including gravity, support, collision, and fixation constraints. The constraints are integrated to construct intricate interactions and form the foundation for the sequence of visual object updates prompted by interactions. In contrast to conventional tool kits (e.g., D3 [1]) that treat the positioning and shaping of visual objects as outcomes of pre-programmed functions, we adopt a physical perspective to model the spatial channels of visual objects. Crucially, our approach introduces spatial updates that are activated by interactions. From this standpoint, the stable positioning of visual objects emerges from the equilibrium reached through the interplay of spatial constraints, inspired by the concept of object equilibrium.

To validate the spatial constraint model, we have developed a prototype system for the interactive manipulation of existing visualizations. After manipulation, the visualizations are transformed to converge towards new layouts, helping users explore the visualization and the underlying data. These interactions support a range of user tasks, such as reordering visual objects through dragging to change stacking orders or orientations, zooming or dragging scales to reorganize or rescale axes, and introducing new constraints or modifying existing ones. These operations enable intelligent interactions that support user analysis tasks including navigation, filtering, reordering, re-encoding, and aggregation. After users interact with the visualization, our system maps spatial constraints to forces and moves visual objects toward convergent positions using force-directed optimization. The resulting convergence leads to a new visualization layout. Our model applies to various common visualization types, such as bar charts, area charts, bubble charts, and line charts. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in supporting diverse interactive tasks for common visualizations through real-world examples and user studies. We conducted user experiments with participants with varying levels of expertise in visualization. The experiments showed that the interactions supported by the spatial constraint model are intuitive and easy to understand, and that they facilitate diverse forms of interaction. Therefore, our approach benefits both novice and expert users. The contributions of this work are as follows:

- A spatial constraint model that represents both the positioning and the positional changes of visual objects, while also facilitating intuitive transitions after users manipulate visualizations.

- A prototype system based on the constraint model, enabling users to activate and manipulate static visualizations.

References:

[2] Satyanarayan et al . (2015) Arvind Satyanarayan, Ryan Russell, Jane Hoffswell, and Jeffrey Heer. 2015. Reactive vega: A streaming dataflow architecture for declarative interactive visualization. IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics 22, 1 (2015), 659–668.
